doc.title: DeFranco Buddy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Critics, the clarinet's decline and the 1950s
title: Reichian therapy and warming up his playing
summary: He credits Reichian therapy with freeing him up as a player and speaker.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: So when do you feel that change was happening, like what era . . .
Not long after I read about it. [laughter]
[laughter] So did you feel that there was validity when you read that? I mean that must have . . .

Yeah, there was a certain amount, but there was more distain and hate attached to the articles than there was validity, but there was something truthful about that. And, I did deliberately change, and of course during that time I was going through some mental problems, which everybody, I didn’t realize, but everybody did. Some were open about it and some weren’t. And I was going to a therapist in New York . . . who was a Reichian therapist, Reichian therapist. Have you heard of Wilhelm Reich?

Yeah. And the purpose of that therapy is to open you up – make you see yourself and see the world and try to get away from your inhibitions and your compulsive training and behavior. And in order to be a clarinet player you have to be damn compulsive. You really do. So, this therapy was beginning to work for me. I finally got so that I could speak on a microphone because up to that point I would freeze up. I would see the microphone and that would be it. I couldn’t say anything.
That’s so interesting, as a performing when you’re making your career as a performing. [laughter]
Oh yeah, a lot of people…
You’re facing your fears everyday then.

And I’ve met a lot of people that way, that couldn’t really . . . open up. And so that was beginning to work, so that worked with my playing as well. It kind of opened the avenues of approach and the vistas of performing and playing, musically.

And also, I’d imagine trying to tackle, you know, the type of music that you were playing when you were playing bebop, I mean there is so much for you to stay on top of, it’s very difficult for someone to stay relaxed.
In the midst of bebop on clarinet!

Yeah, and I finally got to the point where it was second nature to me. I could execute the clarinet that way and feel that I can actually make and expressive move and say something with my instrument.
You were melting into your instrument.
True, true. It worked out pretty well.

I really can’t fault the critics though that much. Sometimes they go overboard but we all go overboard with what we believe in. And, if one critic was to have one person that they fall in love with, they love their playing, they think they’re great – everything else goes by the wayside. They’re not interested in anything else. So, I mean, I guess it’s human nature.
